V01-H-001: Before modern engineering, the place where a river could most easily be crossed was among the most valuable sites in any region. Roads from both banks converged on such a crossing, since travellers and carters had no other way to reach the far side without a long detour. Wherever traffic gathered in this way, inns, markets and workshops followed, and a small settlement took shape around the people obliged to pass through. Over the centuries, many such settlements grew into towns whose very names still recall the ford or bridge from which they began.
V01-H-002: Most of what any of us believes about distant places, past events and the workings of our own bodies rests on nothing but the word of other people. One tradition holds that such beliefs are justified only when we have personally confirmed, through our own observation, that the speakers concerned are generally reliable. The difficulty is that no individual could ever perform enough checks to vouch for more than a tiny fraction of the sources on which he or she depends. If that demand were taken seriously, almost all of our knowledge would therefore collapse, which suggests that trust in testimony is a basic source of justification rather than a derived one.
V01-H-003: People asked to estimate how long a task will take tend to underestimate, even when they have often run late on similar tasks before. This pattern, known as the planning fallacy, seems to arise because forecasters picture the specific steps of the job and imagine each going smoothly. What they leave out are the interruptions, delays and mistakes that, though individually unforeseeable, almost always occur somewhere along the way. A simple remedy, accordingly, is to set aside the details of the plan and ask instead how long comparable projects actually took in the past.
V01-H-004: An old explanation of fashion holds that styles begin among the wealthy, who adopt them precisely because others cannot afford to. As cheaper copies spread downward, the style loses its power to mark distinction, and the wealthy abandon it for something new. The theory thus accounts neatly for why fashion never stands still: every act of imitation from below sets off a fresh flight from above. Yet the theory's neatness is also its weakness, for in recent decades many styles have plainly travelled the other way, from street clothing and working dress into expensive boutiques. Even these reversals may confirm the underlying logic, however, since what the affluent borrow from below is often prized because it signals a knowingness that money alone cannot buy.
V01-H-005: For much of the nineteenth century, voters in many countries declared their choices aloud or on coloured ballots that onlookers could easily identify. Landlords, employers and party agents could therefore see exactly how each man voted, and reward or punish him accordingly. The secret ballot changed this not by making bribery illegal, which it often already was, but by making it impossible for a briber to confirm what he had bought. A vote that cannot be verified is a poor investment, and the market in purchased votes withered in many places once the ballot became private.
V01-H-006: Farmers must decide how much to plant months before they learn what the harvest will fetch, and many simply assume that next season's price will match this season's. After a year of high prices, that assumption leads many of them to plant more, and the larger harvest that follows pushes the price down. Expecting the low price to last, they plant less the next season, and the smaller harvest sends the price back up, so that the swing begins again. What sustains the swing is neither the weather nor any change in tastes but the lag between decision and reward, together with the habit of reading the future off the present. If that diagnosis is right, the remedy may lie less in subsidies than in information, since farmers who could see how much was being planted in total would stop treating today's price as a forecast.
V01-H-007: Many ports that flourished in earlier centuries now lie some distance inland, stranded behind marshes and fields. Their fate was usually sealed by the rivers that had once made them prosperous, which carried silt downstream and deposited it where the current slowed. Year by year, these deposits narrowed the channels until the larger ships of later periods could no longer reach the quays. Trade then moved to deeper harbours along the coast, and the old ports, deprived of their purpose, shrank into quiet market towns.
V01-H-008: A long-standing principle in ethics holds that it can be permissible to cause a harm one foresees but does not intend, when it would be wrong to cause the same harm as a goal or a means. Critics object that the line between intending and merely foreseeing is too easily redrawn, since almost any harmful act can be redescribed so that the harm appears incidental. This objection loses much of its force once intention is tested not by how an act is described but by whether the agent's plan would still succeed if, by some fluke, the harm did not occur. By that measure, an engineer who opens a sluice to save a town, foreseeing that fields downstream will flood, succeeds even if the fields happen to stay dry; one who floods them to drive the farmers away does not.
V01-H-009: In a familiar kind of experiment, a scene on a screen is briefly interrupted by a blank flash, and some detail of it is altered during the interruption. Viewers frequently fail to notice even large changes of this sort, such as a building vanishing from the background, unless they happen to be attending to the altered spot. The finding unsettles the common assumption that we hold a detailed, picture-like record of whatever lies in front of our eyes. It suggests instead that the visual system keeps only a sketch, trusting that the world itself will be there to consult whenever more detail is needed.
V01-H-010: Rules about how to eat, which fork to use, when to begin, what never to do with a knife, are often defended today as matters of simple hygiene. Yet many such rules were laid down long before anyone understood how disease spreads, and some, like the ban on resting elbows on the table, have no bearing on cleanliness at all. Their real function seems to have been social: an elaborate code could be learned only through long exposure, and so it marked out those raised in the right households. This would also explain why such codes tend to grow more intricate wherever newcomers can afford to imitate the outward signs of rank, since a distinction that money can buy soon stops distinguishing. None of this means the hygienic reading is simply false, for a code adopted to keep newcomers out may also, by happy accident, keep food and hands a little cleaner.
V01-H-011: The plague that swept across Europe in the middle of the fourteenth century killed a large share of the population within a few years. Those who survived found that their labour had become scarce, and landowners desperate for workers began offering higher wages to attract them. Alarmed by this, authorities in several kingdoms passed laws attempting to hold wages at their old levels. Such laws proved difficult to enforce, however, because employers who needed hands were often among the first to break them.
V01-H-012: In a market for used cars, sellers usually know far more than buyers about whether a particular vehicle is sound or defective. Unable to tell the difference, buyers will offer only a price that reflects the average quality they expect to find. Owners of good cars, who know their vehicles are worth more than that average, are then reluctant to sell, and many withdraw from the market. As they do, the average quality of cars on offer falls, buyers lower their offers further, and the market can shrink until mostly poor vehicles remain.
V01-H-013: When a busy highway runs through the centre of a small town, residents often campaign for a bypass to carry through traffic around it. Once the bypass opens, the main street becomes quieter and safer, and the air along it noticeably cleaner. Yet the same traffic that residents resented also brought customers to the petrol stations, cafes and shops that depended on passing trade. Some of these businesses close within a few years, and the relief of a calmer centre is mixed with the sight of empty shopfronts. The towns that fare best tend to be those that plan for this loss in advance, giving visitors new reasons to turn off the bypass and stop.
V01-H-014: Ordinary moral thinking recognises a class of acts that are good to do but not wrong to omit, such as giving a kidney to a stranger. Some moral theories have difficulty making room for such acts, because they hold that we are always required to do whatever would produce the most good. On that view the generous donor has merely done her duty, and anyone in a position to donate who declines has done wrong. Many find this conclusion so implausible that they treat it as a reason to doubt the theory rather than to revise their admiration for the donor.
V01-H-015: Most people feel that they understand how ordinary devices such as zips, locks and flush toilets work. That feeling rarely survives a request to explain the mechanism step by step, which tends to produce accounts riddled with gaps the explainer had not noticed. What had passed for understanding was, in large part, familiarity: having seen the device work countless times, people mistook ease of recognition for a grasp of how it works. Nor is the mistake mere carelessness, for in daily life the difference between recognising and understanding seldom matters, since what we lack is stored in manuals, repairers and other people.
V01-H-016: In some countries a tip is expected for almost every service, from a restaurant meal to a taxi ride. Where tipping is customary in this way, wages in restaurants and hotels are often set on the assumption that customers will add to them. A visitor who fails to tip in such a place is therefore not being thrifty but, in effect, cutting the pay of the person who served them. Travellers from such places can err in the opposite way abroad, pressing money on workers in countries where service is fully priced and a tip may seem to imply that they need charity.
V01-H-017: Rulers short of money once had a tempting alternative to raising taxes: they could reduce the silver in each coin while keeping its face value unchanged. For a time this produced a handsome profit, since the mint could strike more coins from the same quantity of metal. But people soon noticed that the new coins contained less silver, and they began hoarding the older, purer ones and spending only the debased. As prices rose to reflect the reduced metal in circulation, the ruler's gain melted away, leaving behind a currency that fewer people trusted.
V01-H-018: Many online shops offer free delivery only on orders above a certain value. A customer whose basket falls just short of that figure will often add an item she did not originally intend to buy. From her point of view this feels like a saving, since the extra item seems to cost little more than the delivery charge she has avoided. For the shop, the arrangement is more attractive still, because the threshold is set so that the extra sales it prompts bring in more than the deliveries it gives away. Free delivery, in other words, is less a gift than a bargain struck on the shop's terms, one that the customer pays for in purchases rather than in a separate fee.
V01-H-019: Until the nineteenth century, each town set its clocks by the sun, so that noon came a few minutes earlier in an eastern town than in one further west. This mattered little while travel was slow, since a journey between two towns took long enough to make a few minutes' discrepancy irrelevant. Railways changed that, because a timetable listing departures and arrivals across many stations was nearly impossible to compile if every station kept its own local time. Railway companies therefore adopted a single standard time across their networks, and the public, which increasingly planned its days around the trains, gradually followed.
V01-H-020: How do I know that other people have thoughts and feelings at all, rather than merely behaving as though they do? A traditional answer reasons by analogy: in my own case pain is linked to wincing and crying out, so when others wince and cry out, I infer that they too are in pain. The weakness of this argument is that it generalises from a single instance, my own, which is the kind of inference we would reject in almost any other setting. A better defence abandons the analogy and treats the existence of other minds as a theory, adopted because no rival explains so economically the vast range of what other people say and do. On this view my belief rests not on my own case at all but on the same kind of reasoning that leads us to accept unseen causes elsewhere in science.
V01-H-021: Before choosing between two attractive options, people often rate them as nearly equal in appeal. Once the choice is made, however, their ratings tend to drift apart, with the chosen option rising in esteem and the rejected one falling. A common explanation is that holding a decision while still valuing what was given up is uncomfortable, and revising one's opinions is the easiest way to ease that discomfort. If this is right, the satisfaction people report with their choices partly reflects the choosing itself, not only the merits of what they chose.
V01-H-022: Readers meeting an ancient oral epic for the first time are often struck by its repetitions: the same phrase attached to the same hero, the same line describing every dawn. A modern editor would strike most of them out, on the principle that a good writer never says the same thing twice in the same words. That principle, however, belongs to a culture of the page, in which a writer can pause, revise and consult what has already been written. A singer composing aloud before an audience could do none of these things, and the stock phrases that look like padding were what let him keep the line moving while he thought ahead.
V01-H-023: In the late eighteenth century, chains of towers with movable arms were built across parts of Europe to send messages over long distances. An operator in each tower watched the next one through a telescope and copied the position of its arms, passing the signal along the line. In clear weather a short message could cross a whole country in a small fraction of the time a mounted courier would need. That speed came at a price, however: at night or in fog the towers could not see one another, and the line fell silent.
V01-H-024: Many subscriptions begin with a free trial that converts automatically into a paid plan unless the customer cancels in time. Firms favour this design because a good many customers who meant to cancel simply forget, or put it off until the deadline has passed. Revenue gathered in this way, however, rests on inattention rather than on any judgement by the customer that the service is worth its price. Such income is correspondingly fragile, since customers who notice the charge often leave resentfully, so a firm relying on forgotten renewals may be trading long-term goodwill for short-term revenue.
V01-H-025: Under the older system in England, each parish was responsible for the roads that ran through it, and local inhabitants were required to give a few days of unpaid labour every year to repair them. The arrangement worked tolerably for lanes used mainly by villagers, but it broke down on the main routes, where most of the wear came from carriers and coaches merely passing through. On those routes parishioners had little reason to labour hard on a road whose damage was done by strangers, and the great highways were often in a deplorable state. The turnpike trusts that spread in the eighteenth century addressed this mismatch by charging tolls, so that the cost of upkeep fell on those who caused the wear. The remedy created a grievance of its own, however, for local people making short journeys now found themselves paying tolls on roads they had once mended with their own hands.
